decks.title: Sex Determination and Sex-linked Inheritance
goals: Explain sex determination in humans, birds, honey bees and grasshoppers
Explain sex-linked inheritance of eye and body colour in Drosophila
Work out the inheritance of haemophilia and colour blindness

slides.heading: Sex Determination, Mutation and Genetic Disorders
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how sex is decided, and how genes on the sex chromosomes are inherited.

visual.alt: Flow from sex chromosomes to sex determination and sex-linked inheritance

slides.narration: In 1891, Henking noticed a nuclear structure in insects that he called the X body. It was later found to be a chromosome, the X chromosome. Chromosomes involved in deciding sex are sex chromosomes; the rest are autosomes. Genes carried on sex chromosomes show special patterns of inheritance.

slides.heading: Four systems of sex determination
slides.body_md: In some organisms the **male** makes two kinds of gametes (**male heterogamety**: XX–XY, XX–XO); in others the **female** does (**female heterogamety**: ZW–ZZ). Honey bees use **haplodiploidy**.

slides.narration: In humans and fruit flies, males have one X and one Y chromosome. In grasshoppers, males simply have one X and no partner, so they have one chromosome fewer than females. In birds, it is the female that has two different sex chromosomes, Z and W. Honey bee males come from unfertilised eggs.

slides.heading: Sex determination in humans
slides.body_md: Human females are **44 + XX** and males **44 + XY**. All eggs carry X; half the sperms carry X and half Y. So each child has an **equal chance** of being a girl or a boy, and the **sperm** decides the sex.

slides.narration: Because every egg carries an X chromosome, the sex of the baby depends only on whether the fertilising sperm carries X or Y. Blaming a mother for the sex of her children is therefore scientifically wrong.

slides.heading: Honey bees: haplodiploidy
slides.body_md: In honey bees, sex is decided by the **number of chromosome sets** an individual receives.

visual.alt: Table of sex determination in honey bees

slides.narration: A drone has no father and cannot have sons, but he has a grandfather and can have grandsons. Because the male is haploid, he produces sperms by mitosis, not meiosis.

slides.heading: Quick check: birds
slides.body_md: In birds, which sex is heterogametic?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think of the Z and W chromosomes.

slides.heading: Sex-linked inheritance in Drosophila
slides.body_md: Genes on the X chromosome are **X-linked**. Morgan found that **white eye** in Drosophila is an X-linked **recessive** trait; **yellow body** is another.

rows: All females red; males half red, half white
Half red, half white in both sexes

visual.alt: Table of Morgan’s reciprocal crosses for eye colour in Drosophila

slides.narration: The two reciprocal crosses give different results, a sign that the gene is on a sex chromosome. A son receives his only X chromosome from his mother, so a white-eyed mother has white-eyed sons: the trait passes criss-cross from mother to son.

slides.heading: Haemophilia: an X-linked recessive disorder
slides.body_md: In **haemophilia**, a single protein in the cascade of proteins needed for **blood clotting** is affected, so a simple cut may cause **non-stop bleeding**. The gene is on the **X chromosome**. A heterozygous female (**carrier**) may pass it to her sons.

slides.narration: Haemophilia is far more common in males, who have only one X. A female is affected only if her mother is a carrier and her father is haemophilic, which is very rare. The family pedigree of Queen Victoria shows many haemophilic descendants, because she was a carrier.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a carrier mother
slides.body_md: A carrier woman (X Xʰ) marries a normal man (X Y). What proportion of their sons and of their daughters will be affected or carriers?
bullets: Gametes: mother X or Xʰ; father X or Y.
Sons: X Y (normal) or Xʰ Y (affected), so affected sons $= \dfrac{0.25}{0.5} = 0.5$ of sons.
Daughters: X X (normal) or X Xʰ (carrier), so carrier daughters $= 0.5$ of daughters; none is affected.

visual.alt: Worked table of the four kinds of children of a carrier mother and a normal father

slides.narration: Half the sons inherit the mother’s affected X and are haemophilic; half the daughters inherit it and are carriers like her. No daughter is affected, because each gets a normal X from her father.

slides.heading: Colour blindness
slides.body_md: **Red–green colour blindness** is due to a mutation in genes on the **X chromosome**, causing a defect in the **red or green cone** of the eye, so the person cannot tell red from green. It occurs in about **8 percent of males** but only about **0.4 percent of females**.

visual.alt: Table of colour-blindness outcomes for three kinds of parents

slides.narration: A son of a carrier mother has a fifty percent chance of being colour blind. A daughter is colour blind only if her mother is at least a carrier and her father is colour blind. That is why the condition is so much commoner in men.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a colour-blind father
slides.body_md: A colour-blind man (Xᶜ Y) marries a woman with normal vision who is not a carrier (X X). Predict their children.
bullets: Every daughter receives Xᶜ from the father and X from the mother: **X Xᶜ, carrier**, normal vision.
Every son receives Y from the father and X from the mother: **X Y, normal**.
So the probability of a colour-blind child is 0; all daughters (probability 0.5 of all children) are carriers.

visual.alt: Worked table of children of a colour-blind father and a non-carrier mother

slides.narration: A father passes his X chromosome only to his daughters and his Y only to his sons. So none of his sons can inherit his colour blindness, but all his daughters carry it and may pass it to their own sons.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Male heterogamety: XX–XY (humans, Drosophila), XX–XO (grasshopper); female heterogamety: ZW–ZZ (birds); haplodiploidy (honey bee).
Humans: all eggs X; sperms X or Y in equal numbers; the father’s sperm decides sex.
X-linked recessive: Drosophila white eye and yellow body; criss-cross inheritance.
Haemophilia and colour blindness: X-linked recessive; carrier mothers pass them to half their sons.

visual.alt: Summary table of sex-determination systems

slides.narration: To recap: sex is decided in different ways in different animals. In humans the father decides it. Genes on the X chromosome give characteristic patterns: carrier mothers, affected sons and criss-cross inheritance.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write **chromosome formulae** (44 + XX, 44 + XY) and label **heterogametic** sex.
Use **X Xʰ** style notation in crosses and give results **by sex**.
State why haemophilia is **rare in females**.
Mention **criss-cross inheritance** for X-linked traits.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Write chromosome formulae and name the heterogametic sex. Use clear notation for X-linked crosses and give results separately for sons and daughters. Explain why affected females are rare. And mention criss-cross inheritance.

slides.heading: Mutation and genetic disorders
slides.body_md: Part 2 — changes in DNA and chromosomes, and the disorders they cause.

visual.alt: Flow from mutation to gene and chromosomal changes and disorders

slides.narration: A mutation is a sudden, heritable change in the DNA sequence. It may affect a single gene or the structure or number of whole chromosomes. Mutations, together with recombination, are a source of variation, but many cause disorders.

slides.heading: Spontaneous and induced mutations
slides.body_md: Mutations arise **spontaneously** (from errors in DNA replication or natural causes) or are **induced** by **mutagens**.

rows: Natural errors in replication or repair
Occur at a low natural rate
UV radiation, X-rays and other ionising radiation

visual.alt: Table of spontaneous and induced mutations

slides.narration: Ultraviolet light, X-rays and some chemicals increase the rate of mutation. Mutations in body cells affect only the individual, while mutations in germ cells can be passed on to offspring.

slides.heading: Gene (point) mutations
slides.body_md: A **point mutation** changes a **single base pair**. In a **substitution**, one base replaces another: a **transition** swaps a purine for a purine or a pyrimidine for a pyrimidine; a **transversion** swaps a purine for a pyrimidine or the reverse. **Insertion or deletion** of bases causes a **frameshift**.

slides.narration: A substitution changes at most one codon. But an insertion or deletion of one or two bases shifts the reading frame, so every codon after it is read wrongly, which usually ruins the protein. Inserting or deleting three bases removes or adds one amino acid without shifting the frame.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: naming mutations
slides.body_md: Classify each change in a DNA strand.
bullets: C → T at one position → **substitution, transition** (pyrimidine to pyrimidine).
G → C at one position → **substitution, transversion** (purine to pyrimidine).
One extra A inserted → **frameshift** (insertion).
Three bases deleted together → one amino acid lost; **no frameshift**.

slides.narration: Ask whether a base was replaced, added or removed. For replacements, check whether the new base is of the same chemical class. For additions or deletions, check whether the number is a multiple of three.

slides.body_md: An **autosomal recessive** disorder. The mutant haemoglobin **HbS** polymerises under low oxygen and red cells become **sickle-shaped**. Only **HbSHbS** individuals show the disease; **HbAHbS** are carriers.

slides.heading: Other Mendelian disorders
slides.body_md: Disorders caused by mutation of a **single gene**, following Mendel’s patterns.

rows: Lacks the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine; phenylalanine and its derivatives accumulate in the brain (mental retardation) and are excreted in urine
Reduced synthesis of a globin chain (α-thalassaemia: genes HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16; β-thalassaemia: gene HBB on chromosome 11), causing anaemia
Defect in red or green cones

visual.alt: Table of Mendelian disorders with inheritance and effects

slides.narration: Thalassaemia and sickle-cell anaemia both affect haemoglobin, but differently. Thalassaemia is a quantitative problem, too little of a normal globin chain. Sickle-cell anaemia is a qualitative problem, an abnormal chain.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: two carrier parents
slides.body_md: Both parents are carriers of sickle-cell anaemia (HbAHbS). What are the chances that a child is (a) affected, (b) a carrier, (c) normal?
bullets: (a) Affected (HbSHbS) $= 0.25$.
(b) Carrier (HbAHbS) $= 0.5$.
(c) Normal (HbAHbA) $= 0.25$.

visual.alt: Worked table of probabilities for children of two carriers

slides.narration: Each parent passes on the normal or the sickle allele with equal chance. One child in four is expected to be affected, two in four carriers and one in four normal. These odds apply afresh to each pregnancy.

slides.heading: Quick check: sickle cell
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about sickle-cell anaemia.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which amino acid replaces which?

slides.heading: Chromosomal disorders
slides.body_md: Caused by **absence, excess or abnormal arrangement** of chromosomes, often from **failure of chromatids to segregate** (non-disjunction) during cell division. Gain or loss of a chromosome is **aneuploidy**; failure of cytokinesis after telophase gives **polyploidy**, common in plants.

rows: Short stature, small round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth, broad palm with a characteristic crease, retarded physical, psychomotor and mental development
Overall masculine development with some feminine features such as gynaecomastia; sterile
Sterile females with rudimentary ovaries and lack of other secondary sexual characters

visual.alt: Table of three chromosomal disorders

slides.narration: Down’s syndrome was first described by Langdon Down in 1866. Klinefelter’s syndrome arises from an extra X in a male, and Turner’s syndrome from the absence of one X in a female. These conditions affect whole chromosomes, not single genes.

slides.heading: Quick check: chromosomal disorders
slides.body_md: A person has 45 chromosomes with a single X and no Y. Which syndrome is this?
slides.narration: Quick check. Count the sex chromosomes.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Mutation: spontaneous or induced (UV, X-rays, chemicals).
Point mutations: transition, transversion; insertion or deletion causes frameshift.
Sickle-cell anaemia: GAG → GUG at codon 6 of β-globin, glutamic acid → valine; autosomal recessive.
Phenylketonuria and thalassaemia: autosomal recessive; colour blindness and haemophilia: X-linked recessive.
Chromosomal: Down’s (trisomy 21), Klinefelter’s (XXY), Turner’s (XO); non-disjunction, aneuploidy, polyploidy.

visual.alt: Summary table of three disorders and their types

slides.narration: To recap: mutations range from a single base to whole chromosomes. Single-gene disorders follow Mendelian patterns, while chromosomal disorders come from too many or too few chromosomes, usually after non-disjunction.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: For sickle-cell anaemia, give the **codon change** and the **amino-acid change**.
Give the **karyotype** for each chromosomal syndrome.
Classify each disorder as **autosomal or X-linked**, dominant or recessive.
Distinguish **transition** from **transversion**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. State the codon and amino-acid change for sickle-cell anaemia. Give the karyotype of each syndrome. Classify each disorder by its pattern of inheritance. And keep transition and transversion apart.

notes.title: Sex Determination, Mutation and Genetic Disorders — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Sex determination
sections.body_md:
In **1891** Henking traced a specific nuclear structure through spermatogenesis in some insects; half the sperms received it and half did not. He called it the **X body**; it was later identified as the **X chromosome**. Chromosomes involved in determining sex are **sex chromosomes**; the rest are **autosomes**.

- **Male heterogamety, XX–XY:** females XX, males XY (humans, *Drosophila*). Human females are **44 + XX** and males **44 + XY**. All eggs carry X; sperms carry X or Y in equal numbers, so the **sperm decides the sex** and each child has a 50 percent chance of either sex.
- **Male heterogamety, XX–XO:** in many insects such as the **grasshopper**, females have two X chromosomes and males **one X** and no Y, so males have one chromosome fewer.
- **Female heterogamety, ZW–ZZ:** in **birds**, females are **ZW** (two kinds of eggs) and males **ZZ**, so the **egg decides** the sex.
- **Haplodiploidy:** in **honey bees**, a fertilised egg develops into a **female** (queen or worker, diploid, 32 chromosomes) and an **unfertilised egg** develops into a **male** (drone, haploid, 16 chromosomes) by **parthenogenesis**. Males produce sperms by **mitosis**; they have no father and cannot have sons, but have a grandfather and can have grandsons.

The sex that produces two kinds of gametes with respect to sex chromosomes.

sections.heading: 2. Sex-linked inheritance
sections.body_md:
Genes on the **X chromosome** (with no counterpart on Y) are **X-linked**; males, with one X, express any X-linked allele they carry (they are **hemizygous**).

**Drosophila.** Morgan found the **white-eye** allele to be X-linked recessive: red-eyed female × white-eyed male gives all red-eyed F1, and an F2 in which all females are red-eyed but half the males are white-eyed. In the reciprocal cross (white-eyed female × red-eyed male), F1 females are red-eyed and males white-eyed — **criss-cross inheritance** from mother to son. **Yellow body** is another X-linked recessive trait.

**Haemophilia** — X-linked recessive. A single protein involved in the cascade of proteins for **blood clotting** is affected, so a simple cut may result in **non-stop bleeding**. Heterozygous females (**carriers**) may transmit it to sons. Affected females are very rare: the mother must be at least a carrier and the father haemophilic. The family of **Queen Victoria**, a carrier, shows many haemophilic descendants.

**Colour blindness** — X-linked recessive mutation in genes for the **red or green cones**, so the person fails to discriminate red and green. It occurs in about **8 percent of males** and only about **0.4 percent of females**. A son of a carrier woman has a 50 percent chance of being colour blind; a daughter is colour blind only if her mother is at least a carrier and her father colour blind.

**Key rules:** a father passes his X to **all daughters** and his Y to **all sons**, so fathers never pass X-linked traits to sons; sons get their X from the **mother**.

sections.heading: 3. Mutation
sections.body_md:
**Mutation** is a phenomenon that results in alteration of **DNA sequences** and consequently in changes in the genotype and phenotype. Besides recombination, mutation is a source of **variation**.
- **Spontaneous** mutations occur naturally, for example through errors in DNA replication.
- **Induced** mutations are caused by **mutagens**: physical (**UV radiation**, X-rays and other ionising radiation) and chemical agents.
- Changes in **chromosomes** (loss, gain or rearrangement of segments or whole chromosomes) cause chromosomal aberrations, commonly seen in cancer cells.

**Gene (point) mutations** — change of a single base pair:
- **Substitution:** a **transition** replaces a purine by another purine (A ↔ G) or a pyrimidine by another pyrimidine (C ↔ T); a **transversion** replaces a purine by a pyrimidine or the reverse.
- **Insertion or deletion** of one or two bases changes the **reading frame** from that point onward: **frameshift mutation**. Insertion or deletion of three bases (one codon) adds or removes one amino acid, leaving the reading frame unaltered.
- **Sickle-cell anaemia** is the classical example of a point mutation: a single base substitution at the **sixth codon** of the **β-globin** gene, **GAG → GUG**, replaces **glutamic acid by valine**.

A physical or chemical agent that induces mutations.
Substitution of a purine for a purine or a pyrimidine for a pyrimidine.
Substitution of a purine for a pyrimidine or vice versa.
Insertion or deletion of bases that shifts the reading frame.

sections.heading: 4. Mendelian disorders
sections.body_md:
Disorders determined by alteration or mutation in a **single gene**; their pattern of inheritance can be traced in a pedigree.

- **Sickle-cell anaemia** — **autosomal recessive**. Caused by substitution of **glutamic acid (Glu)** by **valine (Val)** at the **sixth position** of the **β-globin** chain (codon **GAG → GUG**). The mutant haemoglobin (**HbS**) polymerises under **low oxygen tension**, changing red cells from biconcave discs to elongated **sickle** shapes. Only **HbSHbS** individuals show the disease; **HbAHbS** individuals are apparently unaffected **carriers**, with a 50 percent chance of passing on the allele.
- **Phenylketonuria** — **autosomal recessive** inborn error of metabolism. The affected person **lacks the enzyme** that converts the amino acid **phenylalanine into tyrosine**; phenylalanine accumulates and is converted into **phenylpyruvic acid** and other derivatives, which accumulate in the **brain** (mental retardation) and are **excreted in urine** because of poor absorption by the kidney.
- **Thalassaemia** — **autosomal recessive** blood disease caused by mutation or deletion that results in **reduced rate of synthesis** of one of the globin chains of haemoglobin, causing abnormal haemoglobin and **anaemia**. **α-thalassaemia**: production of α-globin affected; controlled by two closely linked genes **HBA1 and HBA2** on **chromosome 16**. **β-thalassaemia**: production of β-globin affected; controlled by a single gene **HBB** on **chromosome 11**. Thalassaemia is a **quantitative** problem (too few globin molecules), while sickle-cell anaemia is a **qualitative** problem (an incorrectly functioning globin).
- **Colour blindness** and **haemophilia** — **X-linked recessive** (section 2).

key_terms.definition_md: A disorder caused by mutation of a single gene.
The mutant haemoglobin of sickle-cell anaemia.
Autosomal recessive lack of the enzyme converting phenylalanine to tyrosine.
Autosomal recessive reduced synthesis of a globin chain.

sections.heading: 5. Chromosomal disorders
sections.body_md:
Caused by **absence, excess or abnormal arrangement** of one or more chromosomes. **Failure of segregation of chromatids** during cell division results in gain or loss of a chromosome(s): **aneuploidy**. Failure of cytokinesis after telophase results in an increase in a whole set of chromosomes: **polyploidy**, often seen in plants. Trisomy is the presence of an additional copy of a chromosome; monosomy, the lack of one chromosome of a pair.

- **Down’s syndrome** — **trisomy of chromosome 21** (47 chromosomes), first described by **Langdon Down (1866)**. Short statured with a small round head, furrowed tongue and partially open mouth; broad palm with a characteristic palm crease; physical, psychomotor and mental development retarded.
- **Klinefelter’s syndrome** — an **additional X chromosome** in a male: **47, XXY**. Overall masculine development, but feminine development (development of breasts, **gynaecomastia**) is also expressed; **sterile**.
- **Turner’s syndrome** — **absence of one X** chromosome: **45, X0**. Females are **sterile**, as the ovaries are rudimentary; lack of other secondary sexual characters.

key_terms.definition_md: Gain or loss of one or more chromosomes due to failure of segregation.
An increase in whole sets of chromosomes, due to failure of cytokinesis.
Presence of an extra copy of one chromosome.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying the mother decides the sex of a child (the father’s sperm does).
- Calling birds male-heterogametic (females are ZW).
- Writing that a father can pass haemophilia to his son.
- Mixing up transition (same class of base) and transversion (different class).
- Giving the amino-acid change in sickle-cell anaemia the wrong way round (glutamic acid is replaced by valine).
- Calling thalassaemia X-linked (it is autosomal recessive).
- Writing Klinefelter’s as XO or Turner’s as XXY.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: karyotypes, codons, the heterogametic sex, a reason in one sentence.
- 2–3-mark questions: X-linked crosses with results by sex; point-mutation types; one disorder with cause and symptoms.
- 5-mark questions in parts: sex determination in four organisms; haemophilia or colour blindness with a cross; sickle-cell anaemia with the codon change and a carrier cross; chromosomal disorders compared.

questions.stem_md: In domestic fowl, a hen produces two kinds of eggs with respect to the sex chromosomes while a cock produces only one kind of sperm. Which sex is heterogametic in birds?
questions.solution_md: Birds show female heterogamety: females ZW, males ZZ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A cell from the testis of a grasshopper shows one chromosome fewer than a cell from the ovary of the same species. What explains this?

options.text_md: Males lose an autosome during development.
Females have an extra Y chromosome.
Males have a single X chromosome and no Y (XX–XO type).
Males are haploid, like drone bees.

questions.solution_md: In the XO type, females are XX and males have only one X — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Why does a male honey bee (drone) have a grandfather but no father?

options.text_md: He develops from a fertilised egg, but his father dies.
He is produced by budding from a worker.
Workers lay all male eggs after mating.
He develops from an unfertilised egg of the queen, whose own father was a drone.

questions.solution_md: Drones arise by parthenogenesis from unfertilised eggs, so they have a mother and a maternal grandfather but no father — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A couple has three daughters, and relatives blame the wife for not having a son. Which statement is scientifically correct?

options.text_md: The wife’s eggs must carry only X chromosomes because she is weak.
The sex of each child was decided by whether an X- or a Y-bearing sperm fertilised the egg.
The wife produces Y-bearing eggs that failed.
Daughters are born when the mother is older.

questions.solution_md: All eggs carry X; the father’s sperm carries X or Y, so the sperm decides the sex — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In 1891, ______ traced a nuclear structure through spermatogenesis in insects and named it the X body.
questions.solution_md: Henking.

questions.stem_md: The body cells of a honey-bee queen have 32 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are present in the body cells of a drone of the same species?
questions.solution_md: A drone develops from an unfertilised (haploid) egg: $\dfrac{32}{2} = 16$.

questions.stem_md: A couple plans four children. What is the probability that all four will be girls? Give your answer as a decimal.
questions.solution_md: Each child is a girl with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$, independently: $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^4 = 0.0625$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In birds, the male parent decides the sex of the chick.

**Reason (R):** Male birds are heterogametic, with ZW sex chromosomes.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: In birds the female is ZW (heterogametic) and decides the sex; males are ZZ. Both statements are false — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Drone honey bees produce their sperms by mitosis, not meiosis.

answer.model_answer_md: Drones are **haploid**, so their cells cannot undergo a reduction division; mitosis gives **haploid sperms** directly.

questions.solution_md: Haploid drones.

marking_scheme.step: Drone is haploid; mitosis keeps n

questions.stem_md: Using the chromosome formulae 44 + XX and 44 + XY, show why the chance of a human baby being a boy is the same as that of being a girl.

answer.model_answer_md: The mother (44 + XX) forms eggs that all carry **22 + X**. The father (44 + XY) forms **two kinds of sperms in equal numbers**: **22 + X** and **22 + Y**. An X sperm with an egg gives **44 + XX (girl)**; a Y sperm gives **44 + XY (boy)**, so each is equally likely (**1 : 1**).

questions.solution_md: Gametes and 1 : 1.

marking_scheme.step: Eggs all X; sperms X or Y equally
XX girl and XY boy in 1 : 1

questions.stem_md: A poultry farmer wants more hens. Explain why choosing a particular cock will not change the proportion of hens hatched, and which parent actually determines the sex of the chicks.

answer.model_answer_md: In birds the **male is ZZ**, so every sperm carries **Z**; the cock cannot influence the sex. The **hen is ZW** and lays **Z eggs and W eggs** in equal numbers; a Z egg gives a **ZZ male** and a W egg a **ZW female**. So the **hen (egg)** decides the sex.

questions.solution_md: Female heterogamety.

questions.stem_md: Describe the mechanism of sex determination in (i) grasshopper, (ii) birds and (iii) honey bees.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Grasshopper (XX–XO):** females have **two X** chromosomes; males have **one X** and no Y, so males have one chromosome fewer; **male heterogamety**.

(ii) **Birds (ZW–ZZ):** females are **ZW** and produce two kinds of eggs; males are **ZZ**; **female heterogamety**.

(iii) **Honey bees (haplodiploidy):** a **fertilised** egg develops into a **female** (diploid); an **unfertilised** egg develops into a **male** (drone, haploid) by parthenogenesis.

questions.solution_md: Three mechanisms.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between male heterogamety and female heterogamety, with one example of each. [2]
(b) Explain sex determination in honey bees, and state the chromosome number of a drone if the queen has 32. [2]
(c) Why is it wrong to blame a mother for giving birth only to daughters? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In **male heterogamety** the male produces **two kinds of sperms** with respect to sex chromosomes, e.g. **humans (XX–XY)** or grasshopper (XX–XO). In **female heterogamety** the female produces **two kinds of eggs**, e.g. **birds (ZW female, ZZ male)**.

(b) Honey bees show **haplodiploidy**: **fertilised eggs** develop into **diploid females** (queen and workers) and **unfertilised eggs** develop into **haploid males** (drones) by parthenogenesis. A drone has **16** chromosomes.

(c) All of a mother’s eggs carry **X**; the child’s sex depends on whether an **X- or Y-bearing sperm** from the father fertilises the egg, so the **father’s sperm** decides the sex.

questions.solution_md: Heterogamety; haplodiploidy; sperm decides.

questions.stem_md: A colour-blind man marries a woman who is neither colour blind nor a carrier. What is the chance that their son will be colour blind?

options.text_md: One-half, because the father is colour blind
Zero, because the father passes his Y, not his X, to his sons
One-quarter, as in a monohybrid cross
All sons, because the gene is dominant in males

questions.solution_md: Sons receive their X from the mother, who is not a carrier — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A white-eyed female Drosophila is crossed with a red-eyed male (white eye is X-linked recessive). What will the F1 be?

options.text_md: All females red-eyed and all males white-eyed

questions.solution_md: Daughters get the father’s dominant X (red); sons get the mother’s recessive X (white): criss-cross inheritance — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In criss-cross inheritance, an X-linked recessive trait passes from

options.text_md: a father directly to his sons
an affected mother to her sons, and from a father through his daughters to his grandsons

questions.solution_md: Sons get their X from the mother; a father’s X reaches grandsons through his carrier daughters — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A boy bleeds for a very long time after a small cut, and tests show that one protein of the blood-clotting cascade is defective. The disorder is most likely

options.text_md: sickle-cell anaemia, an autosomal recessive disorder

questions.solution_md: Haemophilia affects a clotting protein and is X-linked recessive — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Red–green colour blindness affects about 8 percent of males but only about 0.4 percent of females. Why the difference?

options.text_md: The gene is on the Y chromosome.
Females have no cones for red and green.
Males need only one recessive X-linked allele to be affected; females need two.
The allele is dominant in males and recessive in females.

questions.solution_md: Males are hemizygous for X-linked genes, so one recessive allele shows; females must be homozygous — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A woman who is a carrier of haemophilia marries a normal man. What fraction of their sons is expected to be haemophilic? Give a decimal.
questions.solution_md: Sons get X or Xʰ from the mother equally: affected sons $= \dfrac{0.25}{0.25 + 0.25} = 0.5$.

questions.stem_md: A woman who carries the colour-blindness allele marries a colour-blind man. What fraction of their daughters is expected to be colour blind? Give a decimal.
questions.solution_md: Daughters get Xᶜ from the father and X or Xᶜ from the mother: colour-blind daughters $= \dfrac{0.25}{0.5} = 0.5$.

questions.stem_md: Because a human male has only one X chromosome, he is said to be ______ for genes carried on the X chromosome.
questions.solution_md: Hemizygous.

questions.stem_md: Besides white eye, which other trait studied in Drosophila is inherited as an X-linked recessive character?
questions.solution_md: Yellow body, like white eye, is an X-linked recessive trait in Drosophila — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Haemophilia is much commoner in men than in women.

**Reason (R):** Men have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive X-linked allele is expressed.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the single X of males explains the difference — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: A haemophilic daughter can be born only if her father is haemophilic.

answer.model_answer_md: She needs **two** recessive alleles, and one **X must come from her father**, so he must carry Xʰ, i.e. be haemophilic.

questions.solution_md: Father’s X.

marking_scheme.step: Needs Xʰ from father as well as mother

questions.stem_md: A normal-visioned woman whose father was colour blind marries a normal-visioned man. What are the chances that their son and their daughter will be colour blind? Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: She received **Xᶜ** from her father, so she is a **carrier (X Xᶜ)**. Each **son** gets X or Xᶜ from her and Y from his father, so **half the sons** are expected to be colour blind. Each **daughter** gets a normal X from the father, so **no daughter** is colour blind, though half are carriers.

questions.solution_md: Carrier mother; half the sons.

marking_scheme.step: Half of sons; no daughters affected

questions.stem_md: A colour-blind man marries a woman who is homozygous for normal vision. Write the genotypes of their children and state which of them could have colour-blind children of their own.

answer.model_answer_md: Sons: **X Y**, normal — they got their X from the mother. Daughters: **X Xᶜ**, normal vision but **carriers**, because each received Xᶜ from the father. Only the **daughters** can have colour-blind children (half of their sons).

questions.solution_md: Sons normal; daughters carriers.

marking_scheme.step: Sons X Y, daughters X Xᶜ

questions.stem_md: Morgan crossed a red-eyed female Drosophila with a white-eyed male. Show the F1 and F2, and explain how the results show that the eye-colour gene is X-linked.

answer.model_answer_md: **P:** X X (red female) × Xʷ Y (white male). **F1:** **X Xʷ** females and **X Y** males — **all red-eyed**. **F2** (X Xʷ × X Y): females X X and X Xʷ — **all red**; males **X Y (red)** and **Xʷ Y (white)** in **1 : 1**. White eye appears **only in males** of the F2, and the reciprocal cross gives different results, so the gene is on the **X chromosome**.

questions.solution_md: Cross and reasoning.

marking_scheme.step: F2: females red, half males white

questions.stem_md: A colour-blind girl has a mother with normal vision. Work out the genotypes of the girl, her mother and her father, and the chance that her brother is colour blind.

answer.model_answer_md: A colour-blind girl is **Xᶜ Xᶜ**, receiving one Xᶜ from **each parent**. Her **father** gave an Xᶜ, so he is **Xᶜ Y** (colour blind). Her **mother** has normal vision but gave an Xᶜ, so she is a **carrier, X Xᶜ**. A brother gets his X from the mother: **X or Xᶜ**, so the chance he is colour blind is **one-half**.

questions.solution_md: Genotypes and probability.

marking_scheme.step: Father Xᶜ Y; mother X Xᶜ

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by sex-linked inheritance? Why are X-linked recessive traits seen more often in males? [2]
(b) A man with haemophilia marries a woman who is a carrier. Work out the genotypes and phenotypes of their children, by sex, with a Punnett square. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Sex-linked inheritance** is the inheritance of genes carried on the **sex chromosomes**, usually the X. Males have **one X** (they are hemizygous), so a single recessive X-linked allele is **expressed**; females need **two** copies, so they are usually **carriers**.

(b) Xʰ Y × X Xʰ. Gametes: Xʰ, Y and X, Xʰ. Daughters: **X Xʰ (carrier)** and **Xʰ Xʰ (haemophilic)** — **half each**. Sons: **X Y (normal)** and **Xʰ Y (haemophilic)** — **half each**. Overall: normal daughter 0, carrier daughter 0.25, affected daughter 0.25, normal son 0.25, affected son 0.25 of all children.

questions.solution_md: Definition; cross by sex.

questions.stem_md: Which of these base changes in a DNA strand is a transversion?
questions.solution_md: G (purine) to T (pyrimidine) changes the class of base: a transversion; the others are transitions — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Skin cells of farm workers exposed to strong sunlight for years show more DNA changes than cells of indoor workers. The changes are best described as

options.text_md: frameshifts caused by chemical fertilisers only
induced mutations caused by a physical mutagen (UV radiation)

questions.solution_md: UV radiation is a physical mutagen that induces mutations — option (d).

questions.stem_md: One extra base is inserted near the start of the coding sequence of a gene. What is the most likely effect on the protein?

options.text_md: Every codon after the insertion is read wrongly, so the protein is usually non-functional.
The protein is unchanged because one base cannot matter.
An extra amino acid is added and the rest is normal.

questions.solution_md: Inserting one base shifts the reading frame from that point on — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Three adjacent bases forming one codon are deleted from a gene. What happens to the reading frame?

options.text_md: It shifts by three places, changing every later amino acid.
It is unaltered; the protein loses one amino acid.
The gene can no longer be transcribed.

questions.solution_md: Deleting a whole codon removes one amino acid without shifting the frame — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a physical mutagen capable of inducing mutations in DNA?
questions.solution_md: Ionising radiation such as X-rays, and UV radiation, are physical mutagens — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A point mutation in which a purine is replaced by another purine, or a pyrimidine by another pyrimidine, is called a ______.
questions.solution_md: Transition.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In sickle-cell anaemia the sixth amino acid of the β-globin chain is changed from glutamic acid to valine.

**Reason (R):** The mutation is a frameshift caused by the insertion of a base.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: the change is a single base substitution (GAG → GUG), not a frameshift — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between spontaneous and induced mutations, naming two mutagens.

answer.model_answer_md: **Spontaneous** mutations occur **naturally**, for example through **errors in DNA replication**, at a low rate. **Induced** mutations are caused by **mutagens**: physical agents such as **UV radiation** and **X-rays**, and certain **chemicals**.

questions.solution_md: Two kinds; two mutagens.

questions.stem_md: Describe the three kinds of gene (point) mutation — transition, transversion and frameshift — giving an example base change for each.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Transition:** a **purine replaced by a purine** or a **pyrimidine by a pyrimidine**, e.g. **A → G** or C → T.

**Transversion:** a **purine replaced by a pyrimidine** or vice versa, e.g. **A → T** or G → C.

**Frameshift:** **insertion or deletion** of one or two bases, e.g. an extra A inserted, which **shifts the reading frame** so that every following codon is changed.

questions.stem_md: In sickle-cell anaemia, which change occurs in the mRNA codon for the sixth amino acid of β-globin?
questions.solution_md: A single base substitution changes GAG (glutamic acid) to GUG (valine) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A person with sickle-cell anaemia feels breathless at high altitude, and blood smears show many sickled cells. Why do the cells sickle there?

options.text_md: High altitude causes new mutations in red cells.
Cold air shrinks normal red cells.
Mutant haemoglobin HbS polymerises under low oxygen tension, distorting the red cells.
HbS gains extra oxygen and swells.

questions.solution_md: HbS polymerises when oxygen tension is low, changing biconcave discs to sickle shapes — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A newborn’s urine and blood show high levels of phenylalanine and phenylpyruvic acid. Which enzyme is the baby most likely to lack?

options.text_md: The enzyme that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine
The enzyme that converts glucose to glycogen

questions.solution_md: Phenylketonuria results from lack of phenylalanine hydroxylase — option (b).

questions.stem_md: β-thalassaemia is controlled by a single gene HBB. On which chromosome is it located?
questions.solution_md: HBB lies on chromosome 11; α-globin genes HBA1 and HBA2 lie on chromosome 16 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Two patients are anaemic. In one, the globin chains are normal but made in too small an amount; in the other, a normal amount of an abnormal chain is made. Which pair of diagnoses fits?
questions.solution_md: Thalassaemia reduces synthesis of a globin chain; sickle-cell anaemia makes an incorrectly functioning globin — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Both parents are carriers of sickle-cell anaemia (HbAHbS). What is the probability that their child will have the disease? Give a decimal.
questions.solution_md: HbAHbS $\times$ HbAHbS: probability HbSHbS $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.25$.

questions.stem_md: Match each disorder (column I) with its pattern of inheritance or cause (column II).

match_right.text_md: Extra X chromosome in a male

questions.solution_md: Phenylketonuria — autosomal recessive; haemophilia — X-linked recessive; Klinefelter’s — XXY; Down’s — trisomy 21.

questions.stem_md: Explain the cause of phenylketonuria and why the affected child shows mental retardation.

answer.model_answer_md: Phenylketonuria is an **autosomal recessive** disorder in which the child **lacks the enzyme** that converts **phenylalanine into tyrosine**. Phenylalanine accumulates and is converted to **phenylpyruvic acid** and other derivatives, which **accumulate in the brain**, causing mental retardation; they are also **excreted in urine**.

questions.solution_md: Enzyme lack; brain accumulation.

marking_scheme.step: Lacks enzyme converting phenylalanine to tyrosine

questions.stem_md: Describe the cause of α- and β-thalassaemia, naming the genes and chromosomes involved, and state how thalassaemia differs from sickle-cell anaemia.

answer.model_answer_md: Thalassaemia is an **autosomal recessive** disease caused by mutation or deletion that **reduces the rate of synthesis** of one of the **globin chains**, giving abnormal haemoglobin and **anaemia**. **α-thalassaemia** affects α-globin, controlled by **HBA1 and HBA2** on **chromosome 16**; **β-thalassaemia** affects β-globin, controlled by **HBB** on **chromosome 11**. Thalassaemia is a **quantitative** problem (too few globin molecules), while sickle-cell anaemia is **qualitative** (an incorrectly functioning globin).

questions.solution_md: Cause, genes, comparison.

marking_scheme.step: α: HBA1, HBA2 on 16; β: HBB on 11

questions.stem_md: A man and a woman are both healthy carriers of the sickle-cell allele. Using a Punnett square, find the probabilities of each genotype in their children, and explain why carriers are usually healthy.

answer.model_answer_md: HbAHbS × HbAHbS: gametes HbA, HbS from each. Children: **HbAHbA (normal) 0.25**, **HbAHbS (carrier) 0.5**, **HbSHbS (affected) 0.25**. Carriers are usually healthy because the **normal allele** makes enough **normal haemoglobin**; the disease is **recessive** and appears only in **HbSHbS** individuals.

questions.solution_md: Square with probabilities; recessive.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the molecular basis of sickle-cell anaemia, naming the codon and amino-acid change and the type of mutation. [3]
(b) Why do red blood cells of affected persons become sickle-shaped, and why is this harmful? [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Sickle-cell anaemia is an **autosomal recessive** disorder caused by a **single base substitution** (a **point mutation**) at the **sixth codon** of the **β-globin** gene. The mRNA codon **GAG** becomes **GUG**, so **glutamic acid** is replaced by **valine** at the sixth position of the β-globin chain, forming the mutant haemoglobin **HbS**.

(b) Under **low oxygen tension**, HbS molecules **polymerise**, changing the red cells from **biconcave discs** to elongated **sickle-like** shapes. Sickled cells are rigid and pass poorly through **narrow capillaries**, blocking blood flow and causing tissue damage, and they are destroyed quickly, causing **anaemia**.

questions.solution_md: Molecular change; sickling and harm.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Point mutation at codon 6 of β-globin

questions.stem_md: A girl’s karyotype shows 45 chromosomes with a single X and no Y. She has rudimentary ovaries. Which syndrome is this?
questions.solution_md: Turner’s syndrome is 45, X0, with sterile females and rudimentary ovaries — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A child with a small round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth and a characteristic crease across the broad palm has 47 chromosomes. Which chromosome is most likely present in three copies?
questions.solution_md: These features fit Down’s syndrome, trisomy of chromosome 21 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A tall, sterile man shows some development of breast tissue (gynaecomastia). His karyotype is most likely

options.text_md: 46, XY with a point mutation in β-globin

questions.solution_md: Klinefelter’s syndrome (47, XXY) gives masculine development with some feminine features and sterility — option (b).

questions.stem_md: During egg formation, the two chromatids of chromosome 21 fail to separate. What kind of change can this cause in the embryo?

options.text_md: A transition in the β-globin gene

questions.solution_md: Failure of segregation gives gain or loss of a chromosome (aneuploidy) — option (d).

**Assertion (A):** Down’s syndrome results from an extra copy of chromosome 21.

**Reason (R):** The genes for α-thalassaemia lie on chromosome 16.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.

questions.stem_md: Trisomy 21 is named after the physician Langdon ______, who first described it in 1866.
questions.solution_md: Down.

questions.stem_md: An increase in a whole set of chromosomes resulting from failure of cytokinesis after telophase is called ______, and it is often seen in plants.
questions.solution_md: Polyploidy.

questions.stem_md: Compare Klinefelter’s and Turner’s syndromes in respect of karyotype, sex and fertility.

answer.model_answer_md: **Klinefelter’s:** **47, XXY**; a **male** with overall masculine development and some feminine features (gynaecomastia); **sterile**. **Turner’s:** **45, X0**; a **female** with **rudimentary ovaries** and lack of secondary sexual characters; **sterile**.

questions.solution_md: Two syndromes compared.

questions.stem_md: Describe the features of Down’s syndrome and explain how its chromosomal cause arises.

answer.model_answer_md: Down’s syndrome (first described by **Langdon Down, 1866**) is caused by an **extra copy of chromosome 21** (**trisomy 21**, 47 chromosomes). Affected people are **short** with a **small round head**, **furrowed tongue**, **partially open mouth** and a **broad palm with a characteristic crease**; **physical, psychomotor and mental development is retarded**. The extra chromosome arises when chromatids **fail to segregate** (non-disjunction) during gamete formation.

questions.solution_md: Cause, features, origin.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between aneuploidy and polyploidy, explaining how each arises and giving one example of an aneuploid condition in humans.

answer.model_answer_md: **Aneuploidy** is the **gain or loss of one or a few chromosomes**; it arises when **chromatids or homologues fail to segregate** during cell division, e.g. **Down’s syndrome (trisomy 21)**, Turner’s (45, X0) or Klinefelter’s (47, XXY). **Polyploidy** is an **increase in whole sets of chromosomes**; it arises from **failure of cytokinesis after telophase**, and is common in **plants**.

questions.solution_md: Two terms; origins; example.

questions.stem_md:
(a) How do chromosomal disorders differ from Mendelian disorders? [1]
(b) Tabulate the karyotype and two features each of Down’s, Klinefelter’s and Turner’s syndromes. [3]
(c) Why are chromosomal disorders not traced in pedigrees in the way Mendelian disorders are? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Chromosomal disorders** are caused by **absence, excess or abnormal arrangement of whole chromosomes**; **Mendelian disorders** by mutation of a **single gene**.

(b) **Down’s:** trisomy **21** (47); short stature, small round head, furrowed tongue, palm crease, retarded development. **Klinefelter’s:** **47, XXY**; masculine with gynaecomastia; sterile. **Turner’s:** **45, X0**; sterile female with rudimentary ovaries; lacks secondary sexual characters.

(c) They usually arise **anew** from **failure of chromosome segregation** during gamete formation and affected persons are often **sterile**, so they do not follow a regular pattern through families as single-gene traits do.

questions.solution_md: Difference; table; pedigrees.

questions.passage_md: In a family history: a woman (P) with normal blood clotting had a haemophilic father. She married a man (Q) with normal clotting. They had four children: two daughters with normal clotting and two sons, one of whom (R) was haemophilic.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) X Xʰ (carrier)

**(b)** 0.5

**(c)** (i) From his **mother P**: a son receives his **only X** from his mother. From his father Q he received the **Y chromosome**, and Q’s X carries a **normal** allele in any case.

**OR** (ii) All his **sons** will be **normal** (they get his Y and their mother’s normal X); all his **daughters** will be **carriers** (they get his Xʰ and their mother’s X).

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** She received Xʰ from her haemophilic father but clots normally, so she is a carrier — option (a).

**(b)** Daughters get X from Q and X or Xʰ from P: carriers $= \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5$.

**(c)** (i) Mother; father gives Y.

(ii) Sons normal; daughters carriers.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): If R marries a woman who is not a carrier, what will be true of his sons and daughters?

answer.model_answer_md: All his **sons** will be **normal** (they get his Y and their mother’s normal X); all his **daughters** will be **carriers** (they get his Xʰ and their mother’s X).

questions.passage_md:
A genetics clinic examined the karyotypes of three patients.

| Patient | Chromosome count | Sex chromosomes | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| X | 47 | XY | Three copies of chromosome 21 |
| Y | 47 | XXY | Tall male, sterile |
| Z | 45 | X | Female, rudimentary ovaries |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (c) Klinefelter’s syndrome

**(b)** (b) All three

**(c)** (i) Patient X has **Down’s syndrome**: **short stature** with a **small round head**, **furrowed tongue** and partially open mouth, a **broad palm with a characteristic crease**, and **retarded** physical, psychomotor and mental development (any two).

**OR** (ii) During **meiosis**, the two chromatids (or homologues) of **chromosome 21 fail to separate** (non-disjunction), so one gamete receives **two copies**; fertilisation by a normal gamete then gives **three copies** (trisomy).

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** 47, XXY is Klinefelter’s syndrome — option (c).

**(b)** Each has a chromosome gained or lost, not a whole extra set — option (b).

**(c)** (i) Any two Down’s features.

(ii) Non-disjunction.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): State two features you would expect in patient X.

answer.model_answer_md: Patient X has **Down’s syndrome**: **short stature** with a **small round head**, **furrowed tongue** and partially open mouth, a **broad palm with a characteristic crease**, and **retarded** physical, psychomotor and mental development (any two).

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Explain how a gamete with an extra chromosome, like the one that produced patient X, can arise.

answer.model_answer_md: During **meiosis**, the two chromatids (or homologues) of **chromosome 21 fail to separate** (non-disjunction), so one gamete receives **two copies**; fertilisation by a normal gamete then gives **three copies** (trisomy).
